AMA I work as a tech at a state school for the deaf. I am a CODA Both my mom and dad are deaf and so is just about everyone else in my family is as well.
I'm assuming you're not deaf as well? In what ways do you think your family differs from regular families that people might not expect?

No I'm not deaf.There are lots of ways my family growing up differed. One way is racial slurs are very rare I sign language well at least in my family. You were either hearing or not. Growing up in deaf culture I was not aware of such slurs until I moved out and hung out with other Teens. We were in a department store and my friend at the time said there sure we're an awful lot of wetbacks in this store. He then walked off. I thought he was talking about parachute jackets since we were standing by some parachute pants. They were shiny and kind of wet looking. So I looked around for some parachute jackets but I saw none. I couldn't find my friend so I yelled across the store. Hey! Where are these wetbacks? A store clerk then escorted me out of the store and I had no idea why. My friend at the time laughed a lot at me and explained later. I then asked him what all the slurs were so I could refrain from those words in the future. The deaf world is small and color and race has no influence whether you are deaf or not.

what advice can you give someone who wants to get into interpreting for the deaf?

i am planning to get into CSUN here in SoCal by next year. I really enjoy ASL!

Also, english is my second language. (born in mexico) Thx

ASL is my first. Due to movies on VCR tapes being cheaper in other languages early in my life that is all my mom bought and the only audio I got so I didn't exactly learn how to speak early on. At first they thought I was deaf. So I went to a deaf preschool and I started singing with the music. The adults said a lot of stuff and they gave me a hearing test with all the instructions in English. I guess I passed. So I got kicked out of that school and was sent to a hearing school. My mom was furious this I do remember she was upset cause she thought I was keeping it a secret. I could talk to mom but I had no idea what they were saying. The years that followed resulted in me being put in special classes and lots of frustration from my school. Eventually when I was about 7 they sent a speech therapist to my house t work with me one on one. I finally learned English and haven't shut up since. My suggestion is to immerse yourself in using ASL. I don't think there is a better way. Deaf clubs, deaf friends, and just using it instead of talking will help immensely. If your referring to sentence structure just drop all the conjutives and conjunctions and try to remember your facial expression is also part of your signs.

How do you feel about those in the deaf community that could have implants to restore hearing refusing? I even hear that some in the community look down on those that choose that path? Any of thoughts?

Cochlear Implants haven't always been as advanced as they are now. I guess I should say that I am not an expert on this subject so I will try to avoid the science of it. That being said it is more of a generational thing. The elderly deaf were there when cochlear implants started it was and is a surgery and there are risks as with all surgeries. They were big and unorthodoxed. My mom and my uncle called them monsters. They did not work as well as they do now and I know they have improved, but they are still not perfect. They will not work on everyone and if they have any hearing they loose it. Also there is this fear of tech upgrades cause once this is performed there is no turning back if something better comes along. This is what the elder deaf around me think.

Now my cousin who is much younger doesn't care if you have cochlear implants or not. She went to school with lots of kids who had them and they were much smaller then. I am speaking of the cochlear implants of 20 years ago. The processors were worn on the head then.

The children that receive them now are asked questions like how much of a percentage of hearing they currently have and such. There answers decide if they move further and I don't know the procedure after that. What I do know is that not all procedures are success and those children go to school where I work with all the rest. I don't know what the success rate is I just know that they have lost whatever hearing they had.

In my family no one has under gone the procedure. They just don't want to take that gamble.

Those that look down on those that have under gone the procedure and have had a successful result feel as if that person has chosen to leave there deaf culture behind. I said in an earlier post that my family views the world as either your deaf or hearing.

My opinion on cochlear implants is one of communication I am all for getting those families to be able to communicate with each other. If your from a family like mine then there really is no need we are already able to communicate. We even do sign in hand cause one of my cousins is both blind and deaf. Hearing parents who do not know any ASL should make an effort to learn it. Those that qualify for being a candidate for cochlear implants should make the choice there self. I am not comfortable with children receiveing cochlear implants. I just think they should be old enough to understand the risks and make the choice on their own, but that is just my opinion. If they do wait the technology will only get better.

As a deaf person, I wanted to ask: what were some your struggles as a child growing up with deaf parents? How could they have handled it better? I hope that's not too personal to ask, I just want to know how I can do a good job with any future children :) Thanks!

Biggest problem was interpreting for my family at places that i believe I was just too young to be at.

I believe any medical, legal, and bill negotiations need adult interpreters. I was fine at friends, restaurants, and such. Here are a list of some places I wish I wasn't.

  1. at my aunt's yearly pap-smear.
  2. any and every police interaction.
  3. negotiating for better car insurance.
  4. the deathbed of anyone in our family
  5. funeral homes
  6. all courtroom visits.
  7. Hospitals

Most of these places are supposed to get interpreters,but in the spur of the moment, and the interpreters are hours away or not available "my 5yr old son will do." Now I guess on the police one you can't predict when they are going to pull you over or such. The rest I think can be pretty much planned out ahead of time. These places still haunt me to this day with the memories I developed at an early age. Burying your Grandma at 5 and your Uncle at 7 is bad enough, negotiating casket prices and how to pay the bill is too much. Adult Interpreters always told me stuff like "Well they are legally required to get any deaf an interpreters." However hospitals and other places usually say things like "well we ordered one but since your son is here lets just go ahead and get started." That sentence still makes me shudder. My mom would say things like well it's private and I don't want to share with a stranger. I understand that but If I got advise for you this is it.

Wow, I'm sorry you had to go through that. You're 100% right that an adult interpreter should have been there for those situations... Shame on that hospital. Just... shame. Thank you for sharing. I hope you're doing better now.

I am an adult now I tell those stories for humor more than anything now. I did live through it all but I don't dwell on it anymore I got my own kids to dwell on. So yeah I am all better.

Interpreters have a code of ethics to follow. One of those being to always interpret exactly what is said word for word. 5yr old boys do not follow this so when you go in for car insurance negotiation and you get angry and profane and expect your son to repeat what you have said to the agent it comes out something like "She said no thank you." Why? cause everywhere else you have gotten onto him for profanity and he thinks he is smart enough not to use it. So now mom wants him to be profane with the agent so she can express her anger. The boy looks the agent in the eyes and says "My mom said have a nice day." Does the boy tell mom what he said to the agent "NO" is the agent going to tell mom "NO" is the boy going to tell mom "NO" ........ these are reasons to bring an adult to negotiations.
I definitely agree. 5 year old children are not trained interpreters. Glad to hear you're doing well now :)
